  collapse = TRUE,

SIRAP's default `rad_demux()` path runs the RAD engine packaged by `rrad`
directly in R. It requires no separately downloaded executable and performs a
core-API/resource compatibility handshake before processing data. This vignette
also documents SIRAP's older `rad*()` command-line wrappers for users who
deliberately select `backend = "cli"` or need one of the remaining CLI-only
commands. Demultiplexing is the upstream step that produces the corrected reads
the rest of the package builds on: the [Visium HD processing
guide](visium-hd-processing.html) *starts from* RAD output, and this guide shows
how to get there.

The native entry points are `rad_core_info()`, `rad_scan_wl()`, `rad_demux()`,
`rad_reformat()`, and `rad_download_whitelists()`. The preserved camel-case
external-CLI wrappers are `radPath()`, `radList()`, `radPrep()`, `radScanWl()`,
`radDemux()`, `radReformat()`, and `radRun()`, plus `radSrcPath()` and
`updateRad()` for maintaining a source checkout.

Unlike the other guides, this one uses rad's **public simulated test dataset**,
so the native workflow is runnable without private data or a separately built
`rad` binary.

This guide intentionally does not evaluate code during rendering because its
examples download data and write demultiplexing artifacts.

## Setup

SIRAP is currently private, while `rrad` is public. Your GitHub account needs
read access only to SIRAP. Configure the system credential manager once,
without placing a token in source code, a repository URL, or a committed
`.Renviron` file:

```{r private-install}
install.packages(c("gitcreds", "remotes"))
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
remotes::install_github("hjm2217/SIRAP", dependencies = NA)
```

SIRAP pins the public install source for `rrad` to release `v1.2.1`, so no
credential is needed for that dependency. A private SIRAP access problem may
be reported by GitHub as a repository-not-found or 404 error. If installing
from a local SIRAP checkout, use
`remotes::install_local("/path/to/SIRAP", dependencies = NA)`.

The embedded engine currently supports macOS and Linux. Linux builds use
OpenMP when R exposes it. Current macOS builds are serial: requesting more than
one thread produces a warning, and the result records both the requested and
effective thread counts.

```{r setup}
library(SIRAP)

# Everything in this guide writes under one scratch directory.
runDir <- file.path(tempdir(), "rad_demo")
dir.create(runDir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

nproc <- 4
testFastq <- file.path(runDir, "test.fq.gz")
download.file(
  "https://github.com/indianewok/rad/releases/download/test-data-v1/shuffled_S_lr_synth.fq.gz",
  destfile = testFastq,
  mode = "wb"
)
```

## Native RAD (recommended)

`rad_core_info()` shows the exact embedded engine and compatibility contract.
The call fails early if SIRAP and `rrad` do not agree on the core API, resource
schema, required features, or packaged-resource availability. Its upstream
commit plus embedded-source and resource SHA-256 digests identify the exact
engine material used.

```{r native-rad}
rad_core_info()

nativeRun <- rad_demux(
  layout = "sctagger",
  fastq = testFastq,
  out_dir = runDir,
  output = "demo",
  threads = nproc
)

nativeRun$artifacts
nativeRun$stats
nativeRun$provenance$core_handshake
```

`rad_scan_wl()` and `rad_reformat()` are native operations too; their
camel-case counterparts remain only for legacy CLI compatibility.

```{r native-scan-reformat}
scanRun <- rad_scan_wl(
  input = testFastq,
  output_prefix = file.path(runDir, "cells"),
  adapter_seq = "CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT",
  barcode_length = 16L,
  whitelist = "10x_3v3"
)

reformatted <- rad_reformat(
  fastq = nativeRun,
  output_fastq = file.path(runDir, "demo-igblast.fasta"),
  to_fasta = TRUE,
  header_format = "presto"
)
```

The last call is the native equivalent of `seqkit fq2fa`, but it also gives
IgBLAST and pRESTO one unambiguous header contract:
`read_id|BARCODE=value|UMI=value`. Conversion is streamed directly from plain
or gzip-compressed FASTQ; quality strings never need to be loaded into R.

Small resources ship inside `rrad`. Large built-in 10x whitelists stay out of
the package tarball: the first native operation that requests one downloads it
to R's standard per-user cache, verifies the pinned byte count and SHA-256
digest, and then reuses it. Installing the public `rrad` dependency can require
network access while installing SIRAP; loading either installed package never
downloads a whitelist. Most users do nothing beyond naming the kit. To prepare
a machine or shared cluster cache before an offline run, call:

```{r native-resource-cache}
rad_download_whitelists("10x_3v3")
# Or prefetch every downloadable large whitelist:
rad_download_whitelists()

# Optional shared cache location:
options(rrad.cache_dir = "/shared/rad-cache")
# Refuse all downloads after the cache has been prepared:
options(rrad.offline = TRUE)
```

Native runs recalibrate the layout and position map by default, even if the
same output prefix already exists. Set `reuse_cache = TRUE` only when those
files are known to belong to the same layout and input.

Choose either `kit` or `global_whitelist` as the reference barcode source, not
both. Similarly, `auto_whitelist = TRUE` and `custom_whitelist` are alternatives
for selecting the true/sample barcode set. SIRAP rejects either conflicting
combination before RAD starts so the recorded configuration cannot disagree
with the data actually used.

The remainder of this guide describes the explicit legacy CLI surface.

That adapter is intentionally narrow: it accepts RAD CLI 1.0.2, validates the
complete input and output FASTQ streams, reports legacy cache reuse as
uncontrolled, and rejects CLI debug mode because RAD 1.0.2 can otherwise omit
primary reads. These safety passes do not apply to the native backend.

## Point R at the rad Binary (legacy CLI only)

Every wrapper calls `radPath()` to find the `rad` executable. The resolution
order is: an explicit `rad =` argument, then `getOption("SIRAP.rad_path")`, then
the `SIRAP_RAD_PATH` environment variable, then `Sys.which("rad")` (i.e. rad on
your `PATH`). Confirm R can see rad before running anything else.

```{r locate-rad}
radPath()
#> "/Users/you/code/rad/build/rad"
```

If rad is not on your `PATH`, point SIRAP at it once per session and every
wrapper will pick it up:

```{r set-rad-path}
options(SIRAP.rad_path = "/path/to/rad/build/rad")
# or, in your shell before launching R:
#   export SIRAP_RAD_PATH=/path/to/rad/build/rad
```

Don't have rad built yet? If you have a git clone of the
[rad repo](https://github.com/indianewok/rad), `updateRad()` will pull the
latest commit and (re)build the binary for you. `radSrcPath()` finds the source
tree the same way `radPath()` finds the binary (explicit argument,
`options(SIRAP.rad_src=)`, `SIRAP_RAD_SRC`, or by walking up from the binary's
location). Building rad needs `git`, `cmake`, and a C++17 compiler on `PATH` —
see rad's [installation
guide](https://github.com/indianewok/rad/blob/main/docs/installation.md) for the
one-line dependency install on macOS / conda.

```{r build-rad}
updateRad(path = "/path/to/rad")  # git pull --ff-only + cmake build
```

## Inspect Layouts and Whitelists

rad ships read-layout templates and barcode whitelists by *key*. `radList()`
prints the registered keys and the file each one resolves to — start here so you
know what to pass as `layout =` and `kit =`.

```{r list-layouts}
radList(layouts = TRUE)$stdout
#> [layouts]
#> five_prime          .../resources/read_layout/five_prime_read_layout.csv
#> three_prime         .../resources/read_layout/three_prime_read_layout.csv
#> sctagger            .../resources/read_layout/sctagger_sim_read_layout.csv
#> splitseq            .../resources/read_layout/splitseq_read_layout.csv
#> visium              .../resources/read_layout/visium_three_prime_read_layout.csv
#> visium_hd           .../resources/read_layout/visium_hd_read_layout.csv
#> nanopore_rapid_bc   .../resources/read_layout/nanopore_bulk_rapid_bc_read_layout.csv

radList(whitelists = TRUE)$stdout
#> [whitelists]
#> 10x_3v1 10x_3v2 10x_3v3 10x_3v3.1 10x_3HTv3.1 10x_3v4
#> 10x_5v1 10x_5v2 10x_5HTv2 10x_5v3
#> 10x_Vis_V1 ... 10x_Vis_V5
#> splitseq_bc1 splitseq_bc2 visium_hd_bc1 visium_hd_bc2
```

`radList()` returns the listing as a string in `$stdout` (it captures by
default), so you can also grep it programmatically. Quick layout/kit pairings:
`three_prime` + `10x_3v3` for a 10x 3' library, `five_prime` + `10x_5v3` for 10x
5', `splitseq` + `splitseq_bc1`/`splitseq_bc2`, `visium` + `10x_Vis_V1`..`V5`.
Note the underscores — rad expects `"10x_3v3"`, not `"10xv3"`. For an unusual
chemistry, pass a path to your own layout CSV instead of a key; the [Custom Read
Layouts](custom-read-layouts-with-rad.html) guide walks through writing and
validating one from R, and rad's [layouts-and-whitelists
guide](https://github.com/indianewok/rad/blob/main/docs/layouts-and-whitelists.md)
documents the CSV schema (`id, seq, expected_length, type, class, whitelist`).

## Get the Example Reads

rad publishes the simulated scTagger long-read dataset downloaded during setup:
~98,873 reads from 50 known cells, with each read's true 16 bp barcode embedded
in its header. It is the ideal thing to demultiplex first.

## Check the Read Layout

Before demultiplexing, have rad parse the layout and show you how it will
interpret each read. `read_layout = TRUE` just prints the structure; nothing is
written.

```{r prep-layout}
radPrep(layout = "sctagger", read_layout = TRUE)
```

Adding `position_map = TRUE` samples reads and estimates where each layout
element actually lands, with misalignment statistics. This mode needs a FASTQ and
an output base path; rad writes `<output>_layout.csv` and
`<output>_position_map.csv`, which demux will reuse on later runs to the same
directory.

```{r prep-position-map}
radPrep(
  layout       = "sctagger",
  position_map = TRUE,
  fastq        = testFastq,
  output       = file.path(runDir, "sctagger_prep"),
  threads      = nproc
)
```

## Discover Barcodes De Novo (Optional)

`radScanWl()` scans a FASTQ for the barcodes sitting immediately downstream of an
adapter/primer and writes a whitelist (`<output_prefix>.csv` and `.txt`). For the
scTagger reads the anchoring primer is `CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT` and the barcode
is 16 bp. Passing `whitelist = "10x_3v3"` validates the discovered barcodes
against that kit. On this dataset you should recover the 50 true cell barcodes.

```{r scan-wl}
radScanWl(
  adapter_seq    = "CTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT",
  input          = testFastq,
  barcode_length = 16,
  whitelist      = "10x_3v3",
  output_prefix  = file.path(runDir, "scan"),
  threads        = nproc
)
#> ... Final barcodes (TRUE): 50
```

`radScanWl()` also drives rad's split-barcode mode (BC1 + BC2) — set
`bc1_whitelist` (and optionally `bc2_whitelist`, `umi_length`, `offset_min`,
`offset_max`) to scan paired barcodes such as Visium HD. (Internally the wrapper
emits `--whitelist=KIT` rather than a space-separated value, working around a
rad option-parsing quirk so you don't have to think about it.)

## Demultiplex

`radDemux()` is the main event: it loads the layout and whitelists, runs rad's
chunked alignment/extraction, corrects each barcode, and writes the passing reads
with corrected `CB:Z` (cell barcode) and `UB:Z` (UMI) tags in every header. The
`sctagger` layout already names `10x_3v3` as its default whitelist, so the
minimal run needs only a layout, a FASTQ, an output directory, and a prefix.

```{r demux-basic}
radDemux(
  layout  = "sctagger",
  fastq   = testFastq,
  out_dir = runDir,
  output  = "demo",
  threads = nproc
)
```

This writes `demo.fq.gz` (the corrected, tagged reads) plus the whitelist
summaries `demo_whitelist_true.csv` and `demo_whitelist_global.csv` under
`runDir`. On this dataset roughly **33,700 reads pass** the filter, ~71% of them
an exact `CB:Z` match to the barcode in the read header.

When you have a trusted list of real barcodes, hand it to rad as a custom
whitelist to sharpen correction. The scTagger headers carry the ground-truth
barcode (`@<16bp>-<counter>`), so you can build one in a couple of lines of
shell and pass it through:

```{r demux-true}
# Pull the 50 ground-truth barcodes out of the read headers:
#   gunzip -c test.fq.gz | awk 'NR%4==1{sub(/^@/,"");sub(/-.*/,"");print}' \
#     | sort -u | (echo barcode; cat) > true_50.csv

radDemux(
  layout           = "sctagger",
  fastq            = testFastq,
  kit              = "10x_3v3",
  custom_whitelist = file.path(runDir, "true_50.csv"),
  out_dir          = runDir,
  output           = "demo_true",
  threads          = nproc
)
#> ~55,700 reads pass, ~99.9% exact CB:Z match, 50 unique CBs
```

Other knobs worth knowing (all optional arguments to `radDemux()`):

- `bc_correction_mode = "offensive"` (default) or `"defensive"` — how
  aggressively rad reassigns near-miss barcodes.
- `joint_bc_mode = "strict"` — for paired barcodes (e.g. Visium HD), require
  *all* barcode parts to pass. Default is permissive.
- `global_whitelist = ` — a custom global whitelist CSV, as an alternative to a
  bundled `kit`.
- `whitelist_mutation` / `generated_mutation` — edit-distance search space
  (rad default 2 each).
- RAD CLI 1.0.2's `write_dbg = TRUE` path can suppress primary FASTQ records,
  so SIRAP rejects it. Use native `rad_demux(write_debug = TRUE)` to emit the
  debug artifacts safely alongside primary output.
- `max_reads`, `chunk_size`, `log_file` — throughput and logging controls.

Every wrapper returns an invisible list with `status`, `stdout`, `stderr`, and
the `command` it ran. Pass `capture = TRUE` to collect rad's console output into
that list instead of streaming it live — handy in scripts and reports:

```{r demux-capture}
res <- radDemux(
  layout = "sctagger", fastq = testFastq,
  out_dir = runDir, output = "demo", threads = nproc,
  capture = TRUE
)
res$status        # 0 on success
cat(res$stdout)   # rad's full console output
```

A non-zero exit aborts with an informative error by default; set `check = FALSE`
on the low-level path only if you want to inspect failures yourself.

## Reformat the Output

`radReformat()` post-processes a demuxed FASTQ. Two common operations:

Collapse each header down to `QNAME_CB_UB` so the barcode and UMI travel with the
read name through tools that only keep the identifier. `--reformat-header`
rewrites the file in place:

```{r reformat-header}
radReformat(
  fastq           = file.path(runDir, "demo.fq.gz"),
  reformat_header = TRUE,
  threads         = nproc
)
```

Or split the reads into one `.fq.gz` per cell barcode (keyed off the `CB:Z`
tag), which requires an output directory:

```{r reformat-split}
radReformat(
  fastq    = file.path(runDir, "demo.fq.gz"),
  split_bc = TRUE,
  out_dir  = file.path(runDir, "by_barcode"),
  threads  = nproc
)
```

Use `reformat_delim = " "` to join headers with a space instead of an
underscore.

## One-Call Pipeline

`radRun()` chains `radPrep()` → `radDemux()` → (optionally) `radReformat()` in
one call, sharing `out_dir` and `threads` across steps. Extra named arguments are
forwarded to `radDemux()`. This is the convenient front door once you know your
layout and kit.

```{r rad-run}
result <- radRun(
  layout          = "sctagger",
  fastq           = testFastq,
  out_dir         = runDir,
  output          = "demo",
  threads         = nproc,
  do_reformat     = TRUE,
  reformat_header = TRUE
)

result$prep      # radPrep() result
result$demux     # radDemux() result
result$reformat  # radReformat() result (NULL if do_reformat = FALSE)
```

## Visium HD BCR/TCR — the Spatial Case

The reason SIRAP exists is the wonky end of rad's range: long-read targeted
enrichment of BCR/TCR from **Visium HD** data, where each read carries a *paired*
spatial ID (BC1 + BC2) instead of a single cell barcode. The flow is the
same wrappers with a spatial layout and a couple of HD-specific switches.

The `visium_hd` layout already names `visium_hd_bc1` and `visium_hd_bc2` as the
whitelists for its two barcode elements and flags them as a joint barcode, so you
don't pass a `kit` — just switch on `joint_bc_mode = "strict"` so a read is only
kept when *both* barcode halves correct cleanly:

```{r visium-hd-demux}
visiumFastq <- "spatial_bcr_tcr_reads.fq.gz"  # your enriched long reads

visiumRun <- rad_demux(
  layout        = "visium_hd",
  fastq         = visiumFastq,
  joint_bc_mode = "strict",   # require BOTH paired-barcode halves to correct
  out_dir       = "visium_hd_run",
  output        = "spatial",
  threads       = nproc
)
```

Then rewrite the headers in coordinate mode so the spatial ID becomes a
tissue coordinate downstream. The returned object feeds directly into the
two-pass workflow below. `bin_size` sets the target bin in microns (RAD's
default is 2 µm — the finest Visium HD grid):

```{r visium-hd-coordinate}
coordinateRun <- rad_reformat(
  fastq        = visiumRun,
  coordinate   = "vizHD-v1",
  bin_size     = 2,
  output_fastq = "visium_hd_run/spatial-coordinate.fq.gz",
  threads      = nproc
)
```

The Visium HD layout and its paired-barcode whitelists are **experimental** —
validate on a pilot before scaling up.

From here SIRAP runs two deliberately separate IgBLAST passes. The first
assigns V/D/J calls to every RAD read and provides the aligned receptor region
used for read-level filtering. pRESTO then groups those reads by the spatial
barcode and builds consensuses. The second IgBLAST pass annotates those
consensus sequences, and `MakeDb.py` carries the pRESTO `BARCODE` field into
the final AIRR table.

```{r rad-to-spatial-airr}
processed <- processSpatialSample(
  input_fasta = coordinateRun,
  output_dir = file.path(runDir, "processed"),
  receptor = "ig",
  germline_glob = "/path/to/imgt/human/vdj/imgt_human_*.fasta",
  igblast_base = "/path/to/igblast",
  muscle_exec = "/path/to/muscle",
  nproc = nproc
)

processed$artifacts$read_igblast_airr
processed$artifacts$consensus_fasta
processed$artifacts$final_airr
```

For the read-level pass, `nproc` is a total CPU budget rather than a
per-process multiplier. SIRAP streams complete FASTA records into
approximately base-balanced chunks and runs up to four IgBLAST processes at
once. For example, `nproc = 12` uses four processes with three IgBLAST threads
each. Small inputs stay on the single-process path, and AIRR rows are merged
back in original input order. Direct `runIgblast()` callers can set
`max_processes = 1` to force monolithic execution or supply `chunk_bases` when
benchmarking alternative chunk sizes. In `processSpatialSample()`, use
`igblast_max_processes` to tune or disable the worker pool.

The [Visium HD processing guide](visium-hd-processing.html) continues from the
final AIRR artifact to barcode-grid mapping, tissue coordinates, and spatial
analysis.

## Keeping rad Up to Date

rad moves quickly, and newer builds grow capabilities beyond the ones wrapped
here — for example a `correct-umi` subcommand for per-cell UMI correction, and
support for seqspec YAML layout files in `prep`/`demux`. `updateRad()` keeps your
binary current:

```{r update}
updateRad()                 # git pull --ff-only + rebuild if the commit changed
updateRad(force_rebuild = TRUE)
```

Any rad subcommand — wrapped or not — is reachable: `radHelp("demux")` prints a
subcommand's help from R, and the wrappers accept extra raw CLI tokens through
`...` for flags SIRAP hasn't surfaced yet.
